new_people.draft_wikitext:
[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]
== Biography ==
'''William Glasgow''' of Killycurragh, County Tyrone, is named as the paternal grandfather in the undated family letter preserved as PRONI T1959/3. It reports his marriage to an unidentified Miss Cunningham of Omagh, five sons and three daughters, and sons James and Samuel who remained on the family farm.<ref name="FamilyLetter">Public Record Office of Northern Ireland, T1959/3, photocopy of an undated and unsigned family letter among papers of the 1890s; Albert Rutherford transcription reproduced by Gary Harding, [https://www.genealogy.com/forum/surnames/topics/rutherford/5445/ Rutherfords and Glasgows in Co. Tyrone, Ireland], 9 January 2005. Earlier reviewed account reused on 20 October 2026; original uninspected, online transcription unavailable (HTTP 403) at recheck.</ref>

His birth, death and birthplace are unknown. The letter reports his father as an older William of Killycurragh; the selected Scottish profile candidate is possible, 36%. The reported parental home was Killycurragh; no exact property or life dates are inferred. The family’s 1796 ministerial generation establishes historical context, not a recorded date for William.<ref>[https://cotyrone.com/churchrecord/ministers-pres.html Presbyterian Ministers in Co. Tyrone], John Glasgow from Orritor, ordained New Row 8 March 1796, died 13 July 1801; derivative compilation.</ref>

== Research Notes ==

=== Killycurragh generations, 20 October 2026 ===

The freshly read published transcription of PRONI T1959/3 distinguishes an older William of Killycurragh, the writer’s paternal great-grandfather, from his son William, the writer’s paternal grandfather and husband of Miss Cunningham. The younger William is the Cunningham husband, whose sons included James and Samuel. His son John married Margaret Glasgow after ordination at Coleraine and died at his father’s house in Orritor in July 1801. The surviving child, the anonymous writer, was born five months later; Margaret died in 1817. The separate church compilation identifies John Glasgow from Orritor, ordained at New Row, Coleraine, on 8 March 1796 and dead on 13 July 1801. The shared ministry, origin, name and death month strongly identify the husband. The writer separately describes Margaret’s father William as a son of James Glasgow and Margaret Rutherford; the two parental lines must not be collapsed into one grandfather.

Select [[Glasgow-1318|William Glasgow]] as the possible father of the letter-defined Cunningham husband at 36%. The letter supplies an older Killycurragh William, son of the Tullycoll/Tullyall William and brother of James (husband of Margaret Rutherford) and John (husband of Anne Mason). The 1705 Kirknewton child William has a named father William and a generation compatible with being grandfather of the minister ordained in 1796. The 1702 John baptism supplies a compatible second named son in that Scottish father cluster; the existing James-1025 family supplies the Irish James comparison. This is a positive but non-exclusive family-cluster hypothesis. The Scottish child’s adult identity and migration remain unproved. The 36% includes that identity uncertainty; it is not a confident Scottish–Irish bridge.

Select the letter-defined William of Killycurragh as Rev. John Glasgow’s father at 94% (strongly supported). The writer explicitly gives the writer’s father John, the writer’s paternal grandfather William and his Cunningham marriage. John’s Coleraine ordination, Orritor origin and July 1801 death match the separate New Row minister entry. This concerns the minister’s record-defined identity; it does not identify his grandfather with a Scottish baptism or upgrade his brothers’ later-profile matches.

Select [[Glasgow-2426|William Glasgow]] as Margaret Glasgow’s probable father at 84%. That profile represents William, son of [[Glasgow-1025|James Glasgow]] and Margaret Rutherford, which matches the letter’s maternal-grandfather family position. The letter explicitly names the eldest daughter Margaret as the minister’s wife and the writer’s mother. The profile’s circa-1735 birth and circa-1829 United States death are inherited claims, not exclusionary records and not corrected here. The letter calls William an eldest son; the circa-1735 estimate conflicts with the earlier estimated births of his attached brothers. Those unverified estimates require checking and are preserved here. This is the maternal grandfather, distinct from the Cunningham husband. Original records and an independent adult-life bridge remain to be found.

These are exact subjective assessments of complete relationship-and-identity propositions, not measured probabilities. The family letter is undated and unsigned and is read through Albert Rutherford’s published transcription of a photocopy, not an inspected PRONI original. The minister list is a derivative compilation whose independence from the family tradition is unproved. The Scottish adult identities remain possible: neither the letter nor the 1705 baptism supplies a migration, occupation, property or witness bridge between Kirknewton and Tyrone. The letter’s three-son family and second-cousin statement are internally consistent clues from one source, not independent corroborations. Existing people, vital fields and mothers are preserved. Miss Cunningham and Anne Rutherford are reported maternal names, not transferred to existing maternal profiles. The letter’s first-settler story is family tradition, not proof of the first Glasgow in Tyrone or of the surname’s origin.<ref name="KillycurraghGenerations20261020">PRONI T1959/3, [https://www.genealogy.com/forum/surnames/topics/rutherford/5445/ published transcription], read 20 October 2026; original uninspected. [https://cotyrone.com/churchrecord/ministers-pres.html Minister compilation], John Glasgow, New Row; derivative entry, not an original register.</ref>


Prefer the William named in PRONI T1959/3 as James Glasgow-4145’s probable working father, at 82% confidence. The letter’s paternal uncle James lived and died on the Killycurragh farm, matching the name, specific locality, generation and deceased status of the probate subject indexed at Killycarragh on 21 March 1836. The letter supplies the parent relationship absent from that index. The whole match remains inferred because the original probate document is lost and the letter is derivative; another local James remains possible.<ref name="FamilyLetter" />

Prefer the William named in PRONI T1959/3 as Samuel Glasgow-1698’s probable working father, at 66% confidence. The positive case combines the expressly named Samuel in the letter, the exact Killycurragh family-farm setting, and the later Samuel’s documented farmer/probate household there in 1857. It replaces an unnecessary blanket hold with a testable family placement. The identity is less secure than James’s: there is no traced lease succession or age for the letter’s Samuel, and the current birth estimate may represent a later generation.<ref name="FamilyLetter" />

The percentages assess each entire father-to-profile proposition, including identification of the named son with the later profile; they are subjective comparative judgments, not measured frequencies. The original letter and holding succession remain unverified. Samuel’s circa-1800 birth is an estimate, and a materially older Samuel or a later same-name descendant is possible. His wife Anne’s approximate 1801 birth and their children in the 1820s–1830s do not date Samuel himself. A nephew or later tenant could share the name and townland. Do not transfer a recorded relationship to a later adult merely from the letter’s parent clause. William’s birth and death remain unknown; his named father’s Scottish profile identity is now possible at 36%, and his mother is unidentified. Miss Cunningham is retained as William’s reported wife, without selecting her as either profile’s mother. No existing person is merged or redated, and no live WikiTree edit has been made.

Identity remains unresolved before creating a separate WikiTree profile. This is a documentary account for the working family, not a conclusion that William is a new unique person.

[[Glasgow-2426]] — The current James/Margaret Rutherford parentage instead fits the letter’s maternal grandfather; selected as Margaret’s probable father at 84%. Do not collapse the two grandfathers. This remains an alternative for the paternal grandfather only if that profile’s family placement is wrong.

[[Glasgow-2915]] — Compatible Cookstown-area father generation if the estimated 1760 birth is earlier. His reported wife Margaret Mitchell differs from Miss Cunningham; a prior marriage is possible but unproved. Missing family fields are not an exclusion. No selected identity or ancestral transfer follows.

Inspect PRONI T1959/3 and associated family papers; test William’s identity against existing candidates and trace the Killycurragh holding through leases, rentals and valuation revisions. Establish Samuel’s age independently. The 1836 index date is probate information, not James’s exact death date.

[https://glasgow.phenotype.dev/free-space/glasgow-of-killycurragh-early-c19-aa9477/ Killycurragh household study and current family discussion].

new_people.draft_wikitext:
[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]
{{Ireland Native}}
{{Estimated Date}}
== Biography ==

John Glascow, also recorded as Glasco, was born in Dublin about 1784. He entered Trinity College Dublin on 10 June 1800, aged 16, as a sizar. The college entry names his father Thomas and describes him as Artifex, a craftsman. John became a scholar in 1803 and received a B.A. in the spring term of 1805.<ref>[https://search.findmypast.co.uk/record?id=IRE%2FIE0004%2F364&parentid=IRE%2FIE0004%2F364%2F009 Burtchaell and Sadleir, Alumni Dublinenses (1924), printed p. 328, Findmypast image 364: John Glascow (Glasco) and Manasses Glascow; original printed page inspected 21 October 2026].</ref>

== Research Notes ==

Select [[Glasco-144|Thomas Glasco]] as the Trinity student John’s probable working father at 63% subjective confidence. The original college entry names father Thomas, described as Artifex (craftsman), and says John was born in Dublin. The preferred existing account is the Dublin Thomas already tentatively identified with the watchmaker active in 1773–1783. The uncommon full name, same city, appropriate adult generation and actual craft occupation together make that account a better fit than name and age alone. A further family clue is the 1784 Dublin baptism of John, son of Thomas Glasco and Eliza Hynes: the 1779 watchmaker’s marriage names Miss Hynes. The directory independently supplies Thomas’s forename and the exact Ormond Quay address of the watchmaker; the bracketed Thomas in the marriage extraction is editorial, not another independent name statement.

Prefer the 1784 St Michan’s baptism and the 1800 Trinity student as one John at 72% subjective confidence. Both name John Glasco/Glascow, father Thomas and Dublin; the college age of 16 on 10 June 1800 puts a literal birth window at 11 June 1783–10 June 1784, compatible with a later 17 September 1784 baptism but not a recorded birthday. The Hynes marriage/baptism correspondence and the father’s craft description give the proposed family more specificity than a date-and-name match. The Catholic baptism and scholarship in 1803 leave a material religious-history gap: contemporary accounts describe exclusion of Catholics from scholarships. A baptismal affiliation need not remain unchanged throughout life, but no conversion or mixed-marriage history has been found or inferred. Another John or another Thomas remains possible.<ref>[https://www.findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=IRE%2FPRS%2FBAP%2F3212705&tab=this Findmypast, Ireland Roman Catholic Parish Baptisms, IRE/PRS/BAP/3212705: John Glasco, 17 September 1784, St Michan’s, Dublin; Thomas Glasco and Eliza Hynes; transcript inspected, original uninspected; NLI microfilm 08829-08, image 0083]. [https://eddiesextracts.com/extracts1700/snl1773_99.html Saunders’s News-Letter, marriage extraction under 19 July 1779: watchmaker Glasco of Christchurch Lane to Miss Hynes of Ormond Quay; forename Thomas is editorial in this extraction]. [https://www.swilson.info/wat1783tr.php?brw=sur&brwkey=Glasco Watson’s 1783 Dublin directory, merchants and traders, p. 40 line 1: Thomas Glasco, watchmaker, 20 Ormond Quay; maintained transcription reused]. [https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/commons/1834/may/08/catholics-and-trinity-college-dublin House of Commons, 8 May 1834, Catholics and Trinity College, Dublin: contemporary discussion of the continuing exclusion from scholarships; contextual evidence, not a record of John’s religion].</ref>

Select the record-defined Eliza Hynes as John’s probable mother at 72%, conditional on the preferred baptism-to-student identity. The baptism transcript expressly names her as mother of its John; the college page names no mother. Her identification with the watchmaker’s 1779 Miss Hynes is a further probable comparison, not a recorded marriage for this named Eliza. No marriage to [[Glasco-144|Thomas Glasco]] is installed, and the Duffy, Catherine and Mary King households retain their own identities and grades.

The 63% father estimate assesses the whole link to the modern [[Glasco-144|Thomas]] account, including its unresolved watchmaker identification; it is lower than confidence that the printed student had a father named Thomas. [[Glasco-173|Thomas]]’s 1760 Sarah/Catherine household, [[Glasco-143|Thomas]] and an unrepresented namesake remain alternatives. [[Glasco-173|Thomas]] has no independently recorded trade in the reviewed baptism. The baptism is a Findmypast transcript, not an inspected original; North Anne Street is the church/parish description, not a proved family address. These subjective percentages are not measured frequencies or independent values to multiply. John’s later identity remains on HOLD: [[Glasgow-3946|John Glascow]], died at Thurles 1871 aged 87, and [[Glasgow-3751|John Glasgow]] of the 1820 Abbeville census remain compatible comparisons. No identity merge, live WikiTree edit, exact birth date, father replacement or new connection between existing profile components is claimed.

Inspect the 1784 original baptism for sponsors and address, obtain the specific 1871 Thurles death certificate for occupation and informant, and trace the 1805 graduate into clergy, professional or other records. A surviving compatible candidate prevents new WikiTree creation. Check the 1779 marriage original and further Dublin household records before treating Miss Hynes as named Eliza or transferring spouses between Thomas profiles.

[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]
== Biography ==
'''Jane''' was named as the wife of Thomas Glasgow among defendants in a case brought by David Rynd, Esq., in the Irish Court of Exchequer. The bill-book entry is dated 8 March 1713 as written. Her maiden surname, age, birthplace, parents, marriage date and death have not been established. Dublin is the court venue, not an established residence.<ref name="Exch1713">National Archives of Ireland, Equity Exchequer Bill Books 1712–1714, volume 18, facing left page opposite p.231, 8 March 1713 as written, image 583; [ https://search.findmypast.co.uk/record?id=IRE%2FCOURT%2FEXCHEQUER%2F007635140%2F00583&parentid=IRE%2FCOURT%2FEXCHEQUER%2F0001416171 Findmypast original image]. Original inspected 21 October 2026; the Glasgow entry is on the left page, while the provider indexes right-page number 231.</ref>

== Research Notes ==
The 1713 plaintiff is David Rynd, not the formerly published Lloyd reading. The clearly written David and John Rynd names in the 27 January 1712 entry allow the 1713 surname to be reread as Rynd. Jane’s wife clause is unchanged. The 1712 and 1718 Rynd entries consolidate the Thomas litigation sequence but add no maiden name or maternity evidence.

Prefer [[Glasgow-3556|Thomas Glasgow of Lifford and Donegal]] as her husband, probable at 88% subjective confidence for the complete spouse attachment. The 1713 husband identification is separately assessed at 89%. William Humphrys also appears with the established Thomas in the 1701 Exchequer case; the Moffett network adds context. No residence or estate is stated in the new entry. Another Thomas or a succeeding generation remains possible. The entry's literal “Jane his wife” wording is documented (99%); that is not 99% confidence in the Lifford identification.

No child is assigned to Jane merely because she was Thomas’s wife in 1713.

'''Identity on HOLD:''' the public project catalogue and current anonymous WikiTree captures were checked on 21 October 2026. [[Unknown-719146|Janet Unknown]], mother of Robert recorded at Currie in 1646, survives as a weak older-generation comparison; her circa-1626 birth is an estimate and no spouse is attached. There is no positive Currie–Donegal bridge, but absent later fields do not exclude her. No merge or new live profile is proposed until this comparison is resolved. Thomas's fresh public profile has no spouse attached. This draft represents the woman in the 1713 record, not an identified maiden-name family.

== Sources ==

The 1686 John Hamilton comparison supports the older Donegal cluster indirectly. Assess the husband identification at 89% and the whole Jane-to-Lifford spouse attachment at 88%, probable; the literal marriage wording within the 1713 case is documented, 99%. These are subjective, dependent judgments, not multiplied independent probabilities. The 1713 entry supplies no residence, estate, maiden surname, marriage date, age, parents or children. An unrepresented namesake or succeeding Thomas remains possible. The Edinburgh graduate Thomas-3413 may be the same man, not an independently established competing Irish Thomas. Jane is not assigned as mother of Nathaniel, George, James or any other child. Archibald–Thomas remains 86%; no paternal edge, birth date, merge or live WikiTree edit changes. The court venue Dublin is not either spouse’s residence. Register dates are retained as written; no modern-calendar conversion of the March date is asserted. Janet Unknown-719146 remains a weak unresolved earlier-generation comparison; identity is held rather than merged.

[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]
== Biography ==
'''Lillias Stewart''' was named with Samuel Glasgow in Barony marriage banns dated 24 February 1790. The transcript does not supply a separate wedding date.<ref name="Barony 1790">Church of Scotland, Barony Old Parish Registers, OPR 622/7, item 1, p 42, 1778–1819; [https://www.findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=SCOT%2FOPR%2FMAR%2F0124150%2F1&tab=this Findmypast, Samuel Glasgow and Lillias Stewart, banns 24 February 1790]. Transcript inspected 21 October 2026; original uninspected.</ref>

The same parent pair, with the mother spelled Lilias Stewart, is named in James Glasgow’s 1790 Govan baptism. The matched pair and closely spaced entries favour one household across the two parishes.<ref name="Govan 1790">Church of Scotland, Govan Old Parish Registers, OPR 646/2, item 2, p 69; [https://www.findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=SCOT%2FOPR%2FBAP%2F3976076&tab=this Findmypast, James Glasgow, 1790, parents Samuel Glasgow and Lilias Stewart], transcript 22 March; [https://www.findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=R_688515992&tab=this alternative derivative transcript 25 April 1790]. One underlying event with unresolved dates; transcripts inspected 20 October 2026, originals uninspected.</ref>

Select the record-defined Lillias Stewart as the probable mother of James [[Glasgow-1483]] at 86% subjective confidence. The 1790 Govan baptism explicitly names Samuel Glasgow and Lilias Stewart; the independently recorded Barony banns name that same distinctive full parent pair shortly before either disputed baptism date. This supports one local household across the two registers. James’s adult account has a Govan nailer burial in 1833, aged 42, and children Samuel and Lillias with Jean Cunningham. Parish, approximate age and the paired family names favour identification with the 1790 child. The granddaughter’s Lillias name is supporting naming evidence, not proof. Prefer the 1790 banns couple as Samuel [[Glasgow-3063]] and the record-defined Lillias at 82% subjective confidence, including the groom’s identification with the older nailer. The same full parent pair in the Govan baptism and a chronologically compatible local adult household support the match. Samuel’s 1818 burial at 65 fits a father in 1790, but the banns and baptism supply no trade or age to distinguish him from another Samuel. This rates an intended couple in banns, not a proved completed wedding.

Her birth, death and parents are unknown. Stewart is her recorded surname; no source inspected here establishes whether it was her maiden surname. Barony is an uncertain birth-place suggestion from her own banns context, not a recorded birthplace.

== Research Notes ==
The 86% assesses the complete maternity proposition for the adult James, including the child-to-adult identity. It is not the near-certain named maternal role for the indexed 1790 child alone. The baptism dates 22 March and 25 April remain unresolved versions of one underlying event; no original was inspected. The banns identify neither man as a nailer. James’s burial age suggests about 1790–1791 and is not an exact match to the indexed child. A different James or Samuel remains possible. No birth, death, parents or childhood identity is assigned to Lillias from the contributed 1766 estimate. Samuel [[Glasgow-3063]] remains James’s probable father at 78%. The new banns strengthen the documentary household, but do not resolve the older-nailer identity. No father grade, paternal component, vital field or existing spouse/child is changed. The proposed mother and couple share identity premises and are not independent confirmations. Inspect the original Govan baptism for its date, residence and paternal occupation, then the 1814 James–Jean Cunningham marriage and children’s entries for an occupation, witness or lair link. Test the older Samuel’s identity separately. A 1797 Barony Samuel banns entry (OPR 622/7, item 1, p 88) remains unassigned: do not infer a remarriage, Lillias’s death or a second household for this nailer from the shared name alone.

Identity remains on'''HOLD''' before creation or merger. Anonymous WikiTree searchPerson on 22 October 2026 used FirstName Lilias and Lillias, LastName Stewart, with no place or date restriction:16 and 25 returned matches respectively, both complete single pages of 100. Seven Open/non-living compatible-generation or undated profiles were read with their complete biographies and families. No existing profile was positively identified; compatible candidates remain onHOLD. Stewart-39432 has a 1718 baptism and a separate Moir/North Carolina family: at least 72 in 1790, materially inconsistent with the preferred young-mother/adult-James model. The two searches were bounded name-variant searches, not an exhaustive search of all spellings.

* [[Stewart-6792]] — Lillias, Falkirk 1760: compatible childhood with no recorded adult spouse or fate; the profile’s unsourced tree citation provides no bridge to the 1790 Barony bride. Retain as a candidate, not a selected identity.
* [[Stuart-8558]] — Lillias, Aberlour about 1762: compatible generation, but only an unsourced childhood account; no adult household bridge. Missing later fields are not an exclusion.
* [[Stewart-20221]] — Lilias, 1753–1809, daughter of Charles of Shambellie, reported wife of David Staig. The marriage is undated in the inspected biography; a separate spouse alone does not exclude an earlier or later household. No positive Glasgow bridge.
* [[Stewart-27167]] — Lilias Moore Stewart, married William Newbigging at Corstorphine in 1801, died 1832. An earlier 1790 relationship is not excluded by this later marriage; no link identifies her as this bride.
* [[Stuart-5909]] — Lilias Stuart, about 1764, married Alexander Trotter in 1797. An earlier 1790 household is possible; no record joins the two accounts.
* [[Stewart-24113]] — Lilias of Ballachulish, about 1765–1840, has a distinct Dugald Stuart family with a son born 1787. This is a weaker household comparison; the inspected profile does not identify her with the Barony bride.

The contributed FamilySearch account K 81 S-7 JB supplies a 1766 estimate, not a verified birth record.<ref>[https://ancestors.familysearch.org/en/K81S-7JB/lilias-stewart-1766 FamilySearch contributed Lilias Stewart account]; comparison lead, not independent evidence of birth.</ref>

[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]
== Biography ==

'''Abigail Glasgow''' was born on 5 June 1769 and baptized on 18 June 1769 in the Midcalder parish register. The OPR transcript names her parents as Alexr Glasgow and Emilia Glending, archive reference OPR 694/2, item 4, register range 1691–1820.<ref>Findmypast, ''Scotland, Parish Births & Baptisms 1564-1929'', transcript SCOT/OPR/BAP/4589331, https://www.findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=SCOT%2FOPR%2FBAP%2F4589331&tab=this (inspected 22 October 2026; original register image not inspected).</ref> Two companion indexes give the same baptism under Alexander Glasgow and Emilia Glendining.<ref>Findmypast, ''Scotland, Parish Births & Baptisms 1564-1929'', transcript R_686309313, https://www.findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=R_686309313&tab=this (inspected 22 October 2026; original register image not inspected).</ref><ref>Findmypast, ''Scotland, Parish Births & Baptisms 1564-1929'', transcript R_694108409, https://www.findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=R_694108409&tab=this (inspected 22 October 2026; original register image not inspected).</ref>

== Research Notes ==

Agnes Glasgow, baptized at Midcalder on 22 March 1767 to Alexander Glasgow and Emilia Glendinning, was probably Abigail’s sister. The same named parent pair and parish support one family; the parents’ modern profile identities and Agnes’s later identity remain unresolved. This does not establish Agnes Glasgow-32 as that child.<ref>Findmypast, ''Scotland, Parish Births & Baptisms 1564-1929'', transcripts R_686309332 and R_694108410, https://www.findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=R_686309332&tab=this and https://www.findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=R_694108410&tab=this (inspected 22 October 2026; original register images not inspected; two derivative versions of one baptism).</ref>

The three transcripts are compatible versions of one baptism. The mother’s recorded forms Glending and Glendining are retained. Birth location is inferred from the parish context and must be marked uncertain; the transcript gives a birth date but does not separately name the birthplace. The original register image remains uninspected. Her later life and the modern identities of her named parents are unknown.

Duplicate check, 22 October 2026: [[Glasgow-1655|Abigail Glasgow Anderson]] married John Anderson in Ireland in 1759, before this child’s birth, and is a distinct person. Exact Abigail Glasgow and Abigal/Glasgo/Glasco variant searches and local draft checks found no further compatible historical identity. Do not attach her parents solely by name. [[Glasgow-1309|Alexander Glasgow]] remains a regional comparison, not an identified father; a different recorded spouse alone is no exclusion.

new_people.name: Rev. Samuel Glasgow of Stamford
new_people.draft_wikitext:
[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]
{{Scotland Sticker}}
{{Estimated Date}}
== Biography ==

Samuel Glasgow was described as the paternal grandfather of [[Glasgow-959|Dr Sinclair Holden Glasgow]] in the 1887 Welland county history. Sinclair’s father was [[Glasgow-958|William Glasgow]], a Stamford farmer and justice of the peace, then aged 61, whose wife was Mary Elizabeth Lundy. This identifies Samuel as William’s father.<ref name="Welland 1887">''The History of the County of Welland, Ontario'' (Welland: Welland Tribune, 1887), p.559, Sinclair Holden Glasgow family account; [https://archive.org/details/historyofcountyo00murp/page/n573/mode/1up original scan, IA leaf 573].</ref>

The same account calls Samuel a native of Scotland, says he moved at an early age to County Tyrone, was educated for the ministry at Belfast and ordained by that presbytery, and settled in Stamford before the War of 1812.<ref name="Welland 1887" /> Those details remain the county history’s retrospective account; no ordination or migration record has yet been inspected. His exact birth and death dates are unknown.

== Research Notes ==

The father relationship to William is assessed as 95% confident. Samuel’s identity among existing profiles remains unresolved; this is one consolidated evidence account, not authority to create a duplicate or merge people. His wife and parents have not been identified. Scotland is the reported birthplace; Stamford is only a tentative death-place suggestion from his last reported settlement and son’s residence, not a documented death.

Library and Archives Canada describes receipts, accounts and notes of Samuel Glasgow, a Niagara farmer beside the Chippawa River, militia soldier and prisoner in the War of 1812, who died about 1830. This is a compatible geographical and chronological comparison, not an established identification of the minister. Farming does not itself exclude ministry. The eight-page transcript collection remains uninspected.<ref>Library and Archives Canada, Samuel Glasgow fonds, R6229-0-0-E, formerly MG24-I39, item 98738; catalogue description only, [https://recherche-collection-search.bac-lac.gc.ca/eng/home/record?IdNumber=98738&app=fonandcol archive catalogue].</ref>

The county history’s claim that Glasgow city was named after this family and its Douglas romance are unsupported ancestral traditions and do not establish Samuel’s ancestry.

Samuel Glasgow Sinclair’s paternal grandfather. These linked family details identify the William represented by Glasgow-958 and support Samuel as his father. William was reported alive, aged 61, when the account appeared. 95% concerns William’s father as the Samuel named in this specific family account. It does not identify the minister with an existing numbered Samuel profile, validate the reported ministry/Irish migration from independent records, or prove the city-name and Douglas romance printed beside it. new_people.draft_wikitext:
[[Category: Glasgow Name Study]]
== Biography ==

Thomas is indexed as Thomas Glasgo, father of Joseph Glasgo, in a Campbell County, Virginia death entry dated 1 September 1877. Rose is indexed as the deceased’s mother. The deceased was described as a colored farmer aged 80, with birthplace Campbell. The original register image has been inspected; it writes the parents as Thomas & Rose Glasgo and informant J. Glasgo, Son.<ref name="Campbell 1877">"Virginia, Deaths and Burials, 1853-1912", FamilySearch, [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:X5Y6-54C Joseph Glasgo, 1 September 1877], film 2056976, image 45; original Campbell death register, James River District,1877, film2056976, image 45, inspected 23October2026; [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:S3HT-6LS7-3D7 original image].</ref>

The deceased is the preferred, probable identification of [[Glasgow-2573|Joseph Glasgow]], the Richmond-born Roanoke man whose family with Lucy Gilbert is described in the 1866 cohabitation account.<ref name="Roanoke 1866">CSSR, Roanoke College, [https://cssr.roanoke.edu/s/genarchives/item/4703 Joe Glasgow], derived from Roanoke County 1866 cohabitation register, p. 2 line 37; online account inspected 23 October 2026, original not inspected.</ref> The complete Thomas-to-Roanoke-Joseph relationship is assessed as 74% probable. The younger Joseph’s later Campbell household with named siblings and mother Lucy supplies family context; it does not independently name Thomas.

== Research Notes ==

The death index’s age 80 implies about 1797, whereas the 1870 census age 80 suggests about 1790 for the Roanoke man. Campbell and Richmond are different stated birthplaces. The consort column also repeats Unmarried rather than naming Lucy. These unresolved differences prevent a confident identification. Companion indexes of the same death are not additional witnesses.

Thomas’s own dates, birthplace, residence and parents are unknown. The original writes the parents as Thomas & Rose Glasgo; this surname is not proof of Thomas’s birth surname. The naming of Thomas and Rose as parents does not establish a marriage or Rose’s birth surname. No connection to an existing numbered Thomas, an enslaver’s family or a common Y-DNA founder is established.

Glasgo and records J. Glasgo, Son, as informant. The 1866 cohabitation-register-derived account identifies Joe, Lucy Gilbert and nine children. new_people.name: Daniel Glasgow junior, eldest son in1714
new_people.draft_wikitext:
[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]
== Biography ==
Daniel Glasgow junior was the eldest lawful son of [[Glasgow-3322|Daniel Glasgow senior]] and Mary, daughter of John Gamon. He joined his parents in a conveyance to John Nicholls involving80 acres at Richford Swamp in Norfolk County, Virginia. The family was described as of Moyock, North Carolina. All three acknowledged the deed in Norfolk court on17September1714.<ref name="Daniel1714">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QS7-L9PX-XZZZ Norfolk County, Virginia, Deed Book 9 (1710–1717), manuscript pp.332–335; Glasgow family conveyance to John Nicholls, acknowledged17September1714; FamilySearch DGS007645618, entire-film images507–510. Original register inspected25October2026.]</ref>

== Research Notes ==

Daniel junior also witnessed his father’s 15–16 September 1714 lease and release to Thomas Miller. His mother Mary joined the release. This is a further family-network occurrence, not a separate son or a new confidence improvement.<ref name="DanielWillson1714">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QS7-L9PX-X87K Norfolk County, Virginia, Deed Book 9 (1710–1717), pp. 348–350; Daniel Glasgow to Thomas Miller, lease 15 September and release 16 September 1714, acknowledged 17 September 1714; FamilySearch DGS 007645618, images 523–525.]</ref>


The deed explicitly distinguishes father and son and calls Mary junior’s mother. It also recites the4October1693 Gamon will that defines the senior’s identity. Father confidence98%; the documentary parent clause itself99%. Junior’s birth date, wife, children and later identity are unresolved. Born before1693 is a working majority estimate for joining this1714 deed, not a recorded age. Glasgow-1158 remains a compatible comparison, but its inherited Mary-as-wife account instead suggests duplication of senior; it is not automatically junior. The1718–1719 Currituck tax pair is an85% probable continuation of this Moyock family. No mother profile is selected from the unverified Gammon-934 account solely by its modern label.

== Sources ==
<references />
new_people.assessment: The documentary son is distinct from his father. Glasgow-3322 represents the1693 Mary Gamon husband and is therefore the98% confident father identification for this record-defined son. Glasgow-1158 also carries Mary Gammon as wife and may duplicate the senior account; assigning it to junior would turn that wife into his mother without resolving the identity conflict. Keep both current profiles and their existing parents; do not merge or reparent them. == Biography ==

John Cameron Glasgow was an infant child of [[Glasgow-589|Moses Thomas Glasgow]] and [[Pierce-14470|Mary J. Pierce]]. An undated family account attributed to William Melanchthon Glasgow names Lois Ladd, Robert Finley and John Cameron as their three children, then says that John Cameron died at age five months.<ref name="FamilyAccount">''History of the Glasgow Family'', undated typescript attributed to William Melanchthon Glasgow, page 5 of the held six-page scan, [https://www.wikitree.com/photo/pdf/Glasgow-590 original WikiTree-hosted document]. Retrospective family account; child-group paragraph visually checked 26 October 2026.</ref>

The account says that Mary died on 14 March 1846 and left two small children. This context places John's death before hers; it does not provide his calendar birth or death date. Five months is his reported age at death, not an interval before his mother's death. His surviving siblings are identified as [[Glasgow-2357|Lois Ladd Glasgow]] and [[Glasgow-2356|Robert Finley Glasgow]].<ref name="FamilyAccount" />

== Research Notes ==

Birth and death before 14 March 1846 are contextual boundaries, not exact event dates. Cincinnati, Hamilton County, Ohio is a usable uncertain birth and death location from the immediate-family narrative: Moses returned there in June 1839, married Mary there that November, and the account says that the family continued there until 1851. Neither event place is explicitly recorded for John. No exact year such as 1845 is inferred from his age or position in the child list.

This infant is distinct from [[Glasgow-466|John Cameron Glasgow]], whose public profile gives birth on 9 August 1820 and death in 1901, with different parents. A live John/Glasgow API search covered all 446 returned results on 26 October 2026; public family entries for Moses and Mary were also checked. Sparse open candidates [[Glasgow-3848]], [[Glasgow-3849]], [[Glasgow-3853]], [[Glasgow-3856]], [[Glasgow-3859]], [[Glasgow-3861]] remain unassessed until their cited entries establish register type, year, parents or dated later events. The inferred Cincinnati context does not by itself exclude them. Restricted or withheld search fields also leave a duplicate-check access gap. Creation remains on HOLD pending review of any compatible unresolved candidate; missing fields are not grounds for excluding a person.

The parent roles are supported by the explicit retrospective child clause. The father is individually assessed at 95% (29 October 2026), retaining the strongly-supported grade; the mother remains qualitatively assessed. This initial numerical rating adds no new relationship or confidence-gain event. No contemporary birth, baptism, death or burial entry has been inspected. The two held canonical entries are references to the same PDF, not independent witnesses. Martha Thompson married Moses in 1848, after this infant's inferred lifetime; she is not assigned as his mother or stepmother.

He died aged five months. The contextual death-before-14-March-1846 boundary and inferred Cincinnati locations are qualified, not exact event records. Adult Glasgow-466 (1820–1901, different parents) is excluded. All 446 John/Glasgow API results were paginated, but restricted fields prevent complete duplicate exclusion. The record-defined account is retained with supported parent roles; father individually rated 95% on 29 October 2026, mother qualitative; WikiTree creation stays on HOLD. The source is an undated retrospective family typescript; no original infant record was inspected. Six sparse Scottish-birth candidates remain unassessed: Glasgow-3848, Glasgow-3849, Glasgow-3853, Glasgow-3856, Glasgow-3859, Glasgow-3861. Their cited record references (type and year unresolved) and missing parents need inspection; inferred Cincinnati context alone does not reject them. Glasgow-2882 is excluded by its 1863 marriage, Glasgow-2502 by its 1850 census appearance, and Glasgow-4042 by reported survival into 1848. These profile accounts were inspected; their underlying archival images were not newly inspected. A bounded original-record search on 26 October 2026 retained all six Scottish candidates: their references have not been identified as baptisms or marriages, and their spouse assertions have no inspected dates. Three historical burial cards returned by the official Spring Grove locator concern different people, not this infant. The exact full-name locator query returned no result; this does not prove absence from the cemetery. Parent assessments and creation HOLD are unchanged. Initial father probability review on 29 October 2026 retains the strongly-supported grade at 95%; no genealogy or confidence improvement is claimed.
